02Course overview, prerequisite, text

Course overview

MATH 2321 extends the theory of differential and integral calculus to functions of several variables. Topics include vectors, quadric surfaces, vector functions, partial derivatives, cylindrical and spherical coordinate systems, multiple integrals and applications.

Prerequisites

MATH 1220 or equivalent.

Text

Stewart, Multi-Variable Calculus: Early Transcendentals, a recent edition (the 9th is current). Brooks-Cole.

✎ Explanation (added)

The topic list lines up with Stewart chapters 12 to 15: vectors and quadric surfaces (12), vector functions (13), partial derivatives (14), and multiple integrals with cylindrical and spherical coordinates (15). The section-by-section dates are on the Lecture Schedule & Exercises page.

04Attendance, in-class assignments, tutorials

Attendance

Attendance is a course requirement. Come to class prepared to participate.

In-class Assignments

Short, 1–2 questions, on topic of recent or current lecture. You may collaborate with other students; everyone hands in their own assignment and is responsible for their own work: don’t copy — collaborate. May be given at any time, not necessarily during every lecture.

Tutorials

Each tutorial will feature an assignment to complete, with opportunity to work collaboratively with other students, ask questions and receive guidance from the tutorial leader.

✎ Explanation (added)

Because attendance is stated as a course requirement, the UN grade in section 6 applies: missing more than 30% of classes can produce a UN regardless of marks. In-class assignments are unannounced, so they can only be collected by being there.

05Phones

The course material is not easy. Learning mathematics requires extended periods of focused attention. Distractions make learning more difficult. Turn off your phone’s notifications or put your phone away during class.

Test rule

The presence of a phone, tablet, computer, or other electronic device within reach while writing a test will be assumed to be evidence of academic dishonesty, and will result in a grade of zero and referral to the Dean.

✎ Explanation (added)

The rule is about a device being within reach, not about using it. For a test, that means the iPad and phone go in the bag, not on or under the desk.

08Special accommodation and missed work

If you enrol with Accommodation Services, please speak to me about your accommodation so that I can help accommodate you, especially if your accommodation involves something other than or in addition to 1.5 × (time) for tests.

No make-ups

There are no “make-up” assignments, tests, nor final exams. Neither will assignments, tests, nor the final exam be rescheduled due to absence or any other reason, except in the most exceptional of circumstances if reasonably practical.

In exceptional and extenuating circumstances that would directly result in egregious injustice or undue hardship for a student, accommodation in the form of an adjustment of weightings of course assessments may be possible. Communicate with me should such circumstances arise.

✎ Explanation (added)

A missed test is not rewritten. The only remedy the outline mentions is moving that test’s weight onto other assessments, and only in exceptional circumstances that are raised with him directly.

09Communication

Talk to me. Live and in person. Before, during, or after lectures, or during my scheduled office hours. Or speak to me — live and in person! — to arrange a mutually convenient time to meet.

Email is a much less efficient way to get help with exercises, assignments, learning concepts, or getting help with studying for exams than a real live conversation.

You are welcome to send me email, and I might not ignore it. In particular, if there is information or documentation that can be efficiently provided by email please do send it to me. If I don’t reply to your email it is because I would like to have a conversation in person instead. I might forget, so please do not hesitate to speak to me in class about the fact that you sent me an email.

10Math Lab, Blackboard, calculators

Math Lab

The Math Lab is in room 3910. Here there is a team of dedicated tutors available pretty much all day every weekday ready to provide individual help. In other words, Douglas College has hired professional tutors to provide you with one-on-one assistance.

Blackboard

Relevant things will be posted to our course Blackboard page. Point your browser to the Douglas College home page https://www.douglascollege.ca/. On the Douglas College homepage, click “Logins” at top of page, then “Blackboard”. Select “Math 2321” from your list of courses.

Calculators

You will likely find it useful to have a basic scientific calculator on hand at times. A phone app can work just fine. A “graphing calculator” is not required. The Desmos scientific calculator app is fine; it is both free and ad-free. The Desmos graphing calculator app is also good, and is also free and ad-free. These can also be used on the web at the Desmos website.

✎ Explanation (added)

The calculator paragraph is about studying and classwork. It does not say what is allowed during a test, and section 5 rules out any electronic device within reach while writing one, so a phone calculator app is not an option there. Ask him what, if anything, is permitted on tests.

11Academic integrity policy

Academic honesty is expected. Review the College academic honesty policy on-line or refer to the College Calendar. Ignorance of the policy is no excuse. See: https://www.douglascollege.ca/current-students/important-dates-information/academic-integrity-resources

Definition

Academic Integrity refers to the values on which good academic work must be founded: honesty, trust, fairness, respect and responsibility. Academic integrity includes a commitment not to engage in or tolerate acts of falsification, misrepresentation or deception. Such acts of dishonesty violate the fundamental ethical principles of the academic community and compromise the worth of work completed by others.

In particular, this means (bold in the outline)
  • All work you submit in your name, be it an assignment, quiz, test, or exam, must be your own original work.
  • Handing in another person’s work, or the output of “artificial intelligence” software, as if it is your own is a serious act of academic dishonesty.
  • Doing so will result in a score of “0” for the particular assignment and referral to the Office of the Dean of the Faculty of Science & Technology.

12How to get an A · How to be successful

How to get an A

  • To learn mathematics, you must do mathematics.
    Watching someone else solve a problem, or reading a solution to a problem, almost never helps you understand how to do a problem, no more than watching a soccer game helps you become a better soccer player or attending a concert helps you become a better musician.
    A list of exercises for each section of the text that we will be discussing will be provided. Doing these exercises is how you will learn.
  • In addition to getting help from tutors in the Math Lab, it can be helpful to work together with other students in pairs or small groups.
  • Sometimes it’s helpful to take a break from a problem you are stuck on, and return to it later. Sometimes ideas seem to just take some time to “sink in”. So allow time for this — don’t wait until the day before an exam to start studying!

How to be successful

  • To learn mathematics, you must do mathematics.
    Watching someone else solve a problem, or reading a solution to a problem, does not really help you understand mathematics, any more than watching a soccer game helps you become a better soccer player or attending a concert helps you become a better musician.
    Doing the homework exercises, working on and wrestling with problems is how you learn mathematics!
  • In addition to getting help from your tutorial leader and from tutors in the Math Lab, it can be very helpful to work together with other students.
  • If you are going to use software, computational tools, or a LLM, use these wisely to help you understand, not as a replacement for understanding.
  • When stuck, it is often helpful to take a break from the problem, and return to it later. So don’t leave assignments or studying to the day before. Aim to make regular steady progress by working on exercises, assignments, and studying some each day.
✎ Explanation (added)

The outline says nearly the same thing twice under two headings; both are typed here as they appear. The “list of exercises for each section” it refers to is the Lecture Schedule & Exercises sheet, which has its own page: open the exercise list.

13How to get a C, a B, an A

How to get a C
  • Come to most (say, 70%) of the classes
  • Do many of the homework exercises
  • Have a couple conversations with another student about a homework question or two
How to get a B
  • Attend all the classes
  • Do some planning – anticipate when you will be busy and prioritize staying on track with your coursework ahead of time
  • Do all the homework exercises
  • Try a few extra exercises
  • Make sure you understand all the course material; get help with anything that isn’t clear
How to get an A
  • Do everything listed under “How to get a B”
  • Do several more exercises each week
  • Re-do exercises you find difficult
  • Help other students with their homework
✎ Explanation (added)

The three lists stack: each grade keeps the one below it and adds to it. The step from C to B is “many” exercises becoming all of the assigned ones; the step from B to A is going beyond the assigned list and redoing the hard ones.
